title: Hidden Fisher Information in Many-Body Quantum Sensors
authors: Atta ur Rahman, Muhammad Noman, Samira Elghaayda, Saeed Haddadi
abstract: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) determines the ultimate precision of a quantum sensor after optimization over all allowed measurements, but it does not quantify how difficult the optimal readout is to implement. We introduce a moment Fisher hierarchy $F_M^{(k)}$, which measures the fraction of QFI accessible to collective spin moments up to degree $k$, together with a readout-complexity scale $k_{90}$ defined by the minimum degree required to recover $90\%$ of the QFI. Applying this framework to a nonlinear collective-spin sensor, we show that many-body dynamics can preserve large QFI while transferring the optimal readout into high-rank $SU(2)$ tensor sectors inaccessible to low-order collective observables. For system sizes up to $N=100$, first moments access only $\sim 10^{-2}$ of the available QFI, while the degree required to recover $90\%$ of it grows to $k_{90}\simeq 28$. A rank-resolved analysis of the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) under weak damping shows that the nonlinear protocol pushes the optimal readout toward the highest available tensor ranks while strongly depleting its low-rank weight. These results identify nonlinear tangent-space shear as the mechanism behind a finite-size readout-complexity bottleneck in many-body quantum metrology.
summary: This theoretical paper introduces the moment Fisher hierarchy to quantify how much of the ultimate quantum sensing precision (QFI) is lost because the optimal measurement requires complex, high-rank observables. By analyzing a collective spin sensor, the authors demonstrate that nonlinear dynamics effectively 'hides' this information in high-rank tensor sectors, establishing a concrete, measurable readout-complexity bottleneck for quantum metrology.
main_problem: The paper addresses the distinction between the ultimate sensitivity limit set by Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and the practical limitation imposed by the complexity of the required quantum measurement readout.
main_result: Nonlinear dynamics can preserve high QFI but transfer the optimal readout direction into high-rank tensor sectors, making it inaccessible to low-order collective spin measurements, thus creating a measurable readout-complexity bottleneck.
method: The authors introduce the moment Fisher hierarchy ($F_M^{(k)}$) and the readout-complexity scale ($k_{90}$) to quantify the fraction of QFI accessible via low-order collective moments.
model_or_system: The study analyzes a many-body quantum sensor modeled by $N$ spin-1/2 particles evolving under a kicked collective spin Hamiltonian, specifically examining the transition between linear and resonant nonlinear protocols.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), Moment Fisher Hierarchy ($F_M^{(k)}$), Readout-complexity scale ($k_{90}$), and the weight of the Symmetric Logarithmic Derivative (SLD) in different tensor ranks.
important_parameters: System size ($N$), kick strength ($ eta$), and the degree of the moment expansion ($k$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the moment hierarchy provides a diagnostic measure of measurement resource requirements, and that weak damping does not fundamentally alter the high-rank structure of the optimal readout.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the finite-size scaling of the required readout degree ($k_{90}/N$) and show the migration of the parameter tangent's weight towards high tensor ranks in the resonant nonlinear regime.
paper_structure: The paper builds an argument by first defining the moment hierarchy to bridge QFI and measurement complexity. It then applies this to a kicked spin model, contrasting linear and nonlinear dynamics to demonstrate how the latter hides information in high-rank sectors, which is confirmed by analyzing the SLD structure and robustness against weak damping.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for understanding measurement limitations in quantum metrology, showing that the physical mechanism (nonlinear shear) dictates a specific, high-order readout requirement, which is crucial for designing practical quantum sensors.
